claims.text: High-entropy alloys are composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by competition between configurational entropy and enthalpic tendencies toward ordering or phase separation.
At elevated temperature, configurational entropy lowers the relative free energy of chemically disordered solid solutions and makes ordered intermetallic phases less competitive.
Atomic-size mismatch produces severe lattice distortion in the nanoparticles.
Lattice distortion creates high diffusion barriers and reduces atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility inhibits diffusion-driven chemical ordering and phase separation.
If entropy and lattice-distortion effects dominate the enthalpic drive for segregation, the nanoparticles remain single-phase.
A quinary HEA nanoparticle composition can retain structural similarity between 573 and 1000 K.
The nanoparticles are predicted to remain largely single-phase with minimal segregation or ordering throughout operation from 473 to 1923 K.
A sufficiently favorable ordering enthalpy can overcome configurational-entropy stabilization.
When ordering enthalpy becomes too competitive, the nanoparticles may segregate or form ordered phases.
Systems with very small atomic-size differences may fail to retain stability because they have insufficient lattice distortion.
An element with a particularly strong ordering tendency can cause the stability prediction to fail.
Using an inert or otherwise controlled atmosphere prevents external chemical reactions from being mistaken for intrinsic instability.
Temperature-cycled specimens will be compared with their initial homogeneous single-phase baseline.
XRD, HRTEM, and APT can respectively assess phase formation, lattice or phase-boundary structure, and local elemental segregation.
Reproducible formation of distinct ordered, intermetallic, or segregated phases within the predicted stability range would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary permits instability whenever distortion or entropy is insufficient or ordering enthalpy is strong, but these quantities are not operationally thresholded. The falsification rule nevertheless treats phase formation within 473–1923 K as falsifying, so the same result could be characterized either as an allowed boundary failure or as decisive falsification.
